ports.name: Lagos Port Complex (Apapa)
ports.principalFunction: General cargo / container / bulk / RoRo / liquid

point.note: Reliable facility location; the exact coordinate still needs confirmation.

ports.brief:
Nigeria's oldest and historically busiest gateway, sitting on the western side of Lagos Harbour at Apapa. Together with Tin Can Island it has for decades carried the overwhelming majority of Nigeria's containerised and general-cargo trade, serving the Lagos consumption market and the wider national hinterland. The complex operates on the landlord model: NPA holds the infrastructure while five concessioned terminals (bulk, multipurpose, container) work the quay from Berths 1 to 20, flanked by a dense belt of oil, fishery and industrial jetties along the Apapa and Ijora waterfront.

Operationally, Apapa is defined as much by its landside constraints as its marine assets: chronic truck congestion on the port access corridor, aging quay infrastructure and draft limits (~13.5 m at the deepest container berths) cap vessel size and throughput. In NPA's 2025 operational data it handled roughly 16.7% of national cargo throughput, having ceded the lead to Lekki. A federal rehabilitation programme (part of a ~$1bn / £746m UK Export Finance-backed package) targeting berth reconstruction, dredging and automation is the defining medium-term story for this port — monitor works phasing, as berth closures will shift traffic across the harbour.

ports.name: Tin Can Island Port Complex

point.note: Reliable facility location; the exact coordinate still needs confirmation.

ports.brief:
Built in the mid-1970s oil-boom era specifically to relieve Apapa congestion, Tin Can Island sits immediately west of the Lagos Port Complex and is Nigeria's second classic gateway. Its quay is divided among five concessionaires across Berths 1–12 — bulk (Josepdam), container (TICT, Five Star), container/general (PCHS) and West Africa's flagship RoRo operation (PTML) — making it the country's most operator-diverse port on a single breakwater. It consistently records the highest vessel-call count of any Nigerian port (about 22.7% of 2025 arrivals), skewed toward smaller geared vessels and car carriers.

For intelligence purposes Tin Can is the vehicle-import capital of Nigeria and a dense customs-risk environment: high-volume RoRo and used-vehicle flows, groupage containers and adjacent bonded terminals create elevated manifest-discrepancy and valuation-fraud exposure relative to pure box terminals. Like Apapa it is inside the federal port-rehabilitation programme; its shallow drafts (mostly under 11 m) mean it competes on cargo type rather than vessel size, and its long-term role is being reshaped by Lekki's rise.

ports.name: Lekki Deep Sea Port

point.note: Reliable facility location; the exact coordinate still needs confirmation.

ports.brief:
Nigeria's first deep-sea port and the single most consequential change to the country's maritime geography in a generation. Commissioned for commercial operations in 2023 with a 16.5 m natural channel depth, fully automated container handling and capacity for super-post-Panamax tonnage, Lekki removed the vessel-size ceiling that confined Nigerian trade to the old Lagos harbour. Growth has been steep: from 54,289 TEU in its 2023 start-up year to 287,000 TEU in 2024, roughly 50% utilisation of its 1.2m TEU Phase 1 capacity by late 2025, and — on NPA 2025 data — about 40.6% of national cargo throughput, making it Nigeria's largest port by that measure and second by trade value.

Structurally, Lekki is a PPP anchored by Tolaram and China Harbour Engineering with Nigerian public-sector participation, operating inside the Lagos Free Zone next to the Dangote refinery complex — a co-location that makes the Lekki/Ibeju-Lekki axis Nigeria's emerging integrated trade-and-energy corridor. Its principal constraints are landside: evacuation still leans on road and growing barge operations (~10% of cargo movement), with rail integration the key watch-item. Transshipment to Togo, Benin, Ghana and Côte d'Ivoire is building, positioning Lekki as a West African hub rather than a purely national gateway.

ports.name: Rivers Port Complex (Port Harcourt)

point.note: Reliable facility location; the exact coordinate still needs confirmation.

ports.brief:
The historic eastern gateway on the Bonny River estuary at Port Harcourt, and the original port of the Niger Delta trade. Today the Rivers Port Complex is a modest general-cargo, bulk and petroleum-products port whose two concessioned terminals (Berths 1–8) are supplemented by oil jetties, a tank farm and government marine facilities. Its shallow river approach limits vessel size, and much of the region's cargo growth has migrated downriver to Onne.

The port's intelligence significance is disproportionate to its tonnage: it sits inside the Niger Delta security environment, handles petroleum-products flows that intersect with the region's illegal bunkering and fuel-diversion economy, and its concession relationships (PTOL, BUA) have a contested history that requires current verification before being relied on. NPA's nationwide modernisation drive lists Port Harcourt among the ports slated for upgrade procurement.

ports.name: Onne Port Complex

point.note: Reliable facility location; the exact coordinate still needs confirmation.

ports.brief:
Nigeria's energy-logistics super-hub and by several measures its most strategically distinctive port. Located on the Bonny River estuary along Ogu Creek, Onne pioneered the landlord port model in Nigeria and hosts what NPA and OGFZA describe as the world's largest oil & gas free zone — a fabrication, supply-base and marine-logistics ecosystem serving Nigerian and wider Gulf of Guinea offshore fields, with 200+ licensed companies and berthing for the offshore supply-vessel fleet that sustains Niger Delta production. NPA states the port accounts for over 65% of export cargo through Nigerian seaports and, per 2026 reporting, it is now the authority's second-highest revenue port; on 2025 throughput data it handled about 19.1% of national cargo.

The complex splits into the Federal Lighter Terminal (FLT) and Federal Ocean Terminal (FOT), concessioned to Brawal, Intels, WACT and ICTSNL, ringed by LNG, cement, fertiliser, repair and shipyard jetties. For Seaphore, Onne should never be modelled as a container port with extras: it is the logistics heart of Nigeria's upstream sector, meaning vessel traffic is dominated by OSVs, project cargo and rig moves, free-zone customs rules alter cargo-clearance logic, and disruption here propagates directly into national crude production.

ports.name: Bonny

point.note: Reliable facility location; the exact coordinate still needs confirmation.

ports.brief:
Bonny Island is the marine heart of Nigeria's gas economy and one of its two most valuable pieces of coastal energy real estate. The island hosts the Nigeria LNG liquefaction complex and its export jetties, the Bonny crude oil terminal system operated by Shell, and the anchorage and channel infrastructure through which LNG carriers, crude tankers and Onne-bound traffic all pass. The Bonny fairway is arguably Nigeria's single most critical maritime chokepoint: a security or navigational incident here simultaneously threatens LNG exports, crude liftings and the Onne supply chain.

The crude side of Bonny has been chronically stressed by upstream theft and pipeline sabotage — receipts into the terminal have at times collapsed to a small fraction of pipeline nominations, prompting alternative evacuation schemes (including the Nembe FSO route). Any Bonny-related record in Seaphore should therefore carry a high security-risk weighting and be linked to pipeline-incident and force-majeure event feeds.

ports.name: Delta Port Complex (Warri)

point.note: Reliable facility location; the exact coordinate still needs confirmation.

ports.brief:
The administrative parent of Nigeria's western Delta port system, spanning the Old and New ports at Warri plus outstations at Koko, Sapele and Burutu. Warri is a river port on the Escravos/Warri river system serving the western Niger Delta's oil-industry hinterland and general trade; its terminals are multipurpose and its wider directory includes the country's densest inventory of private oil, refinery and industrial jetties (Ifie, Ogunu, Oghara corridors), reflecting the petroleum-products distribution economy around the Warri refinery.

Draft is the defining physical constraint — the river channel and bar restrict vessel size (most private jetties work 5.5–8 m drafts) — and the security environment is materially riskier than Lagos, with a history of militancy, pipeline interference and crude theft in the surrounding creeks. Delta Port is on NPA's modernisation procurement list; for the registry, its value is as the anchor node for a large second-tier facility layer rather than as a headline cargo port.
ports.notes: Niger Delta gateway; parent of Koko, Sapele, Burutu

ports.name: Koko

point.note: Reliable facility location; the exact coordinate still needs confirmation.

ports.brief:
A small Delta-state river port on the Benin River that functions primarily as a petroleum-products and industrial jetty cluster rather than a general-cargo hub. Koko's concessioned terminal (Creekshore) is complemented by oil and energy jetties (Total, Taurus, Optima, Awaritse) working drafts around 7–8 m, serving tank-farm and products-distribution trades for the western Delta.

Koko's history carries a notable environmental-intelligence marker — it was the site of Nigeria's landmark 1980s toxic-waste dumping scandal that shaped national hazardous-cargo regulation — and its products jetties sit within the fuel-diversion risk geography of the Delta. Records here should link to tank-farm ownership and products-movement data.

ports.name: Sapele

point.note: Reliable facility location; the exact coordinate still needs confirmation.

ports.brief:
An NPA-operated river port upstream on the Benin River, historically a timber and agricultural outlet and today a modest multipurpose facility surrounded by industrial jetties (power, flour, feed, steel-adjacent trades) working ~6.4–7.5 m drafts. Sapele Power's jetty and the Life Flour Mills and Bendels Feed facilities define its cargo character: industrial raw-material imports for inland processors.

Because NPA operates Sapele directly rather than through a concession, its commercial data is thinner than the concessioned ports; treat throughput and berth information as requiring direct NPA sourcing. Its strategic relevance to Seaphore is as a feeder node in the Delta river system and a monitoring point for inland-waterway cargo flows.

ports.name: Burutu

point.note: Reliable facility location; the exact coordinate still needs confirmation.

ports.brief:
The most remote of the Delta Port outstations, an NPA-operated river facility deep in the western Delta at Burutu. A significant transshipment town in the colonial palm-produce era, it is today a minimal-activity port whose principal modern relevance is its position on inland waterway routes and its proximity to oil-producing creeks — periodic federal proposals to revive Burutu as a river-port and dockyard hub recur in policy discussion.

For the registry, Burutu is a low-activity, low-data node: coordinates are approximate, no berth/throughput data is verified, and its practical intelligence value is as a geographic anchor for waterway traffic and security monitoring in the Forcados river axis.

ports.name: Calabar Port Complex

point.note: Reliable facility location; the exact coordinate still needs confirmation.

ports.brief:
Nigeria's easternmost seaport, on the Calabar River in Cross River State, operating as a three-terminal concessioned complex (Intels, Ecomarine, Shoreline) handling general, container and liquid-bulk cargo. Calabar serves the southeastern hinterland and cross-border trade toward Cameroon, and hosts an adjacent free trade zone; its Old Terminal retains liquid-bulk infrastructure from its historical Addax relationship.

The port's chronic constraint is its long, siltation-prone river channel: draft limitations have persistently suppressed vessel size and made channel-dredging status the single most important operational variable for any Calabar record. Concession terms here run later than the Lagos ports (Ecomarine extended to 2037), and NPA lists Calabar in its modernisation procurement pipeline.

ports.name: Brass

point.note: Reliable facility location; the exact coordinate still needs confirmation.

ports.brief:
The Brass terminal complex on the Bayelsa coast is an oil-export node in the eastern-central Delta, anchored by the NAOC/Eni-associated Brass crude terminal and its offshore loading system. Brass crude (Brass River grade) has repeatedly been subject to force majeure following attacks on feeder pipelines, making the terminal a bellwether for eastern-Delta security conditions.

Brass also carries forward-looking significance: the site has long been slated for gas-based industrialisation (Brass LNG and methanol proposals), so registry records should distinguish the operating crude system from proposed facilities. Coordinates are port-directory approximations pending verification.

ports.name: Forcados

point.note: Reliable facility location; the exact coordinate still needs confirmation.

ports.brief:
Parent node for the Forcados oil terminal system at the mouth of the Forcados River — one of Nigeria's largest and most incident-prone crude export systems (medium-sweet Forcados grade). The terminal's offshore loading and subsea infrastructure have suffered repeated sabotage-driven shutdowns, including multi-month force majeures and the 2022 discovery of a long-running illegal tapping operation on feeder infrastructure; recent loading programmes put Forcados exports in the ~180,000 b/d range (Nov 2025 schedule).

Model Forcados as a system, not a point: shore tankage, subsea lines and SPM loading points plus the Trans-Forcados pipeline network feeding it. Its operational state is a direct proxy for western-Delta security and a material driver of national export revenue.

ports.name: Escravos

point.note: Reliable facility location; the exact coordinate still needs confirmation.

ports.brief:
Parent node for Chevron's Escravos complex at the Escravos River mouth — a combined crude terminal, gas plant (including the Escravos gas-to-liquids facility) and deep-draft jetty cluster (18 m at the Chevron jetties, the deepest in the Delta directory). Escravos-grade crude loads here, and the associated Escravos gas pipeline system has been a recurring sabotage target with knock-on effects on national power supply.

For Seaphore, Escravos is a dual-class node (oil export + gas processing/export) inside a high-risk security geography; its records should link crude-loading schedules, gas-system incidents and the Chevron corporate layer, and its jetty drafts make it one of the few Delta locations capable of receiving large tankers close inshore.

ports.name: Qua Iboe

point.note: Reliable facility location; the exact coordinate still needs confirmation.

ports.brief:
Parent node for ExxonMobil's Qua Iboe terminal at Ibeno, Akwa Ibom — historically the export point for Nigeria's largest single crude stream (Qua Iboe light, historically 300,000+ b/d; ~158,000 b/d on the Nov 2025 loading programme). The onshore terminal with offshore SPM loading serves the Mobil-operated shallow-water fields off Akwa Ibom and has experienced its own history of force majeure events from pipeline damage and community disruption.

Qua Iboe anchors the eastern end of Nigeria's export geography, away from the core Delta creeks, giving it a somewhat different risk profile — more exposed to open-water piracy and community/industrial action than to creek-based theft. Registry linkage should connect it to the Yoho and Usari offshore systems in the same ExxonMobil production complex.

terminals.name: Terminal A & B (Apapa Bulk)

point.note: This is the parent port's coordinate, not the facility's. The facility is known to be within the port complex, and nothing finer is established.

terminals.brief:
Apapa Bulk Terminals operates Berths 1–5 at the head of the Lagos Port Complex quay, concessioned under the 2006 port-reform wave as the complex's dedicated dry-bulk gateway. Its trade is dominated by food and industrial bulks — grain, sugar, salt, fertiliser and similar commodities feeding the Lagos milling and manufacturing cluster directly behind the port — making it a key node in Nigeria's food-security supply chain.

For analytics, bulk berths behave differently from box terminals: longer berth stays, gearless bulkers dependent on shore/mobile equipment, and cargo volumes that swing with harvest cycles and FX-driven import demand. Quay, draft and equipment specifications are not publicly verified for this terminal and are honestly gapped in the registry; concession renewal status post-2006 also requires verification.

terminals.name: Terminal C & D (ENL)
terminals.primaryCargo: Breakbulk / general / container / vehicles / liquid bulk

point.note: This is the parent port's coordinate, not the facility's. The facility is known to be within the port complex, and nothing finer is established.

terminals.brief:
ENL Consortium runs the largest berth frontage in Apapa — Berths 6–14, an 11-berth multipurpose operation handling breakbulk, general cargo, containers, vehicles and some liquid bulk at drafts of roughly 9.7–11 m. Founded in 2002 by Prince C. A. Haastrup and operating the concession since April 2006, ENL is one of the most prominent indigenous terminal operators in Nigeria, with its own haulage network extending the terminal's reach inland.

Multipurpose terminals like C&D are the shock-absorbers of a port system: they take the cargo that doesn't fit specialised berths (project cargo, steel, bagged goods), which makes their throughput mix a useful indicator of industrial and construction activity. The originally recorded 10+5-year concession term means current tenure status is a live verification item — flag any ENL record as concession-status-sensitive.

terminals.name: APM Terminals Apapa

point.note: This is the parent port's coordinate, not the facility's. The facility is known to be within the port complex, and nothing finer is established.

terminals.brief:
APM Terminals Apapa is Nigeria's flagship legacy container terminal and the country's principal box gateway before Lekki's rise. Operating Berths 15–18A under a 25-year concession (March 2006–March 2031), the A.P. Moller–Maersk subsidiary has invested ~$438m to build a 1,005 m quay, 55 ha paved yard, 900 reefer plugs and a fleet of 27 RTGs and 13 mobile harbour cranes, with rail and barge connectivity and >1m TEU annual capacity at 13.5 m maximum draft.

Its intelligence weight is threefold: it is the benchmark against which Nigerian container efficiency is measured; its 2031 concession expiry is one of the biggest commercial events on the Nigerian ports calendar; and its reefer and rail capabilities make it central to cold-chain and hinterland-evacuation analytics. Berth congestion here historically drove national import-cost inflation — monitoring vessel queues at APM remains a high-signal activity.
terminals.notes: 55 ha yard; 900 reefer plugs; 27 RTG, 13 MHC; rail + barge; ~$438m invested since 2006

terminals.name: Terminal E (Greenview)

point.note: This is the parent port's coordinate, not the facility's. The facility is known to be within the port complex, and nothing finer is established.

terminals.brief:
Greenview Development Nigeria operates Terminal E (Berths 19–20) at the eastern end of the Apapa quay under a 25-year concession running to April 2031. It is a bulk operation in the same commodity ecosystem as Apapa Bulk Terminals, and industry reporting associates it with the Flour Mills of Nigeria group cluster around Apapa — a linkage worth verifying and recording in the company layer because it would tie the berth directly to Nigeria's largest food-processing complex.

Specifications (quay length, draft, equipment) are not publicly verified; the concession end date makes 2031 a clustering point at which four Apapa/Onne-era concessions mature together, a structural event for the whole port system.

terminals.name: Lilypond (Ijora)

point.note: Reliable facility location; the exact coordinate still needs confirmation.

terminals.brief:
Lilypond at Ijora is APM Terminals' inland container facility supporting the Apapa quay operation — historically a bonded container depot and more recently repurposed within the export-processing and empty-container logistics chain for the Lagos port system. It has no quay of its own; its role is decongestion, storage and customs processing off-dock.

For mapping, Lilypond should render as an inland node linked to NG-LAG-T03 rather than a coastal marker, and its status should be verified periodically: Lagos off-dock facilities have been repeatedly re-designated (export processing, truck transit, empty depots) as congestion policy shifts.
terminals.notes: Related inland facility — not a quayside concession

terminals.name: Terminal A (Josepdam)

point.note: Reliable facility location; the exact coordinate still needs confirmation.

terminals.brief:
Josepdam Port Services holds Terminal A at Tin Can (Berths 1, 1A, 2; 484 m of quay), a bulk operation concessioned in May 2006 on an original 10-year term whose renewal status requires verification. Its bulk trade mirrors Apapa's food-and-industrial commodity flows on the Tin Can side of the harbour.

The short original concession term is the analytically interesting feature: 10-year terminals from the 2006 reform have lived through renewal/extension cycles that are poorly documented publicly, so operator tenure should be treated as a monitored variable rather than a settled fact.

terminals.name: Terminal B (TICT)
terminals.operator: Tin Can Island Container Terminal Ltd

point.note: Facility-level coordinate, verified or near-verified.

terminals.brief:
Tin Can Island Container Terminal (TICT) is the anchor box operation at Tin Can, running Berths 3–5 (764.64 m of quay) since June 2006 on an original 15-year term. Industry reporting has long associated TICT with Bolloré/AGL-linked operating interests — a corporate relationship worth confirming for the company layer, as it would connect the terminal to one of Africa's major port networks.

TICT competes directly with APM Apapa and, increasingly, Lekki for Lagos box traffic; its terminal-level coordinates are among the best-verified in the registry, making it a reliable geographic anchor for Tin Can mapping. Concession renewal status post-2021 is a verification item.

terminals.name: Terminal C (PCHS)

point.note: Facility-level coordinate, verified or near-verified.

terminals.brief:
Port & Cargo Handling Services operates Terminal C (Berths 6, 7, 7A, 8; 789.3 m — the longest quay frontage at Tin Can), a container and general-cargo operation concessioned in May 2006. Industry reporting associates PCHS with the SIFAX Group, a major indigenous logistics conglomerate; confirm and record in the company layer.

Its mixed container/general profile makes it a bridge terminal between the pure box operations and the bulk/RoRo berths, and its throughput mix is a useful proxy for the informal-import economy (groupage, consolidated cargo) that characterises much Tin Can traffic. Original 10-year term — renewal status to verify.

terminals.name: Terminal D (Five Star)

point.note: Reliable facility location; the exact coordinate still needs confirmation.

terminals.brief:
Five Star Logistics runs Terminal D (Berths 9–10; 437.03 m), a container and general-cargo operation concessioned in May 2006 on an original 10-year term. It is the smallest quay allocation among the Tin Can concessions and functions as a secondary box/general facility within the complex.

As with its 2006 peers, tenure and any berth reallocation under the federal rehabilitation programme are the live monitoring items; equipment and draft specifications are not publicly verified in this registry.

terminals.name: PTML / New RoRo Terminal

point.note: Facility-level coordinate, verified or near-verified.

terminals.brief:
PTML is West Africa's premier RoRo gateway and the most fully-specified terminal in this registry: Berths 11–12 on a 35 ha site with 500 m of quay, capacity for 400,000 vehicles, 150,000 TEU and 200,000 t of project cargo annually, its own barge fleet (4×1,000 t barges, 5 pusher tugs), 140-camera CCTV coverage and 200 security officers under ISPS. Concessioned in August 2009 for 25 years, it is operationally associated with the Grimaldi Group's West Africa services — verify and record that corporate linkage.

Vehicle imports are among Nigeria's highest-risk cargo classes for valuation fraud, stolen-vehicle trafficking and concealment, giving PTML outsized customs-intelligence importance relative to its tonnage. Its barge operation also makes it a pioneer of water-side evacuation in Lagos — relevant to congestion analytics across the harbour.
terminals.notes: 35 ha site; 3,500 m2 warehouse; 10,000 m2 barge area; 140 CCTV; ISPS

terminals.name: Terminal A

point.note: This is the parent port's coordinate, not the facility's. The facility is known to be within the port complex, and nothing finer is established.

terminals.brief:
Terminal A at Rivers Port (Berths 1–4) is the multipurpose heart of the old Port Harcourt quay, handling liquid bulk, dry bulk and breakbulk. The recorded operator, Ports & Terminal Operators Ltd (PTOL), reflects the 2006 concession round, but Rivers Port concession arrangements have a contested and litigated history — current operating control must be verified before any record here is relied upon.

The terminal's petroleum-products dimension ties it into the Delta fuel-distribution economy and its attendant diversion risks; its river draft constraints keep vessel sizes modest. Treat all specifications as unverified pending direct NPA sourcing.

terminals.name: Terminal B

point.note: This is the parent port's coordinate, not the facility's. The facility is known to be within the port complex, and nothing finer is established.

terminals.brief:
Terminal B (Berths 5–8) at Rivers Port is recorded with a BUA Ports & Terminals association handling liquid bulk and breakbulk — a relationship requiring current verification given the well-documented concession dispute history at this port between BUA and federal authorities. BUA's wider industrial footprint (sugar, cement, flour) makes the berth's bulk flows strategically linked to one of Nigeria's largest conglomerates if the relationship is confirmed.

As with Terminal A, this is a verification-first record: operator, berth condition (portions of the quay historically required reconstruction) and cargo mix all need current sourcing.

terminals.name: Federal Lighter Terminal A

point.note: This is the parent port's coordinate, not the facility's. The facility is known to be within the port complex, and nothing finer is established.

terminals.brief:
Federal Lighter Terminal A is Brawal Shipping's single-berth multipurpose operation at Onne, concessioned 2006–2031 per ICRC records. FLT is the older, shallower inner terminal of the Onne complex, historically handling general and lighter-borne cargo before the FOT's deep-water expansion.

Within the Onne ecosystem Brawal's berth serves general/marine cargo niches alongside Intels' dominant logistics operation; it is a minor node individually but part of the 2031 concession-maturity cluster that will reshape Onne's commercial structure.

terminals.name: Federal Lighter Terminal B

point.note: This is the parent port's coordinate, not the facility's. The facility is known to be within the port complex, and nothing finer is established.

terminals.brief:
Federal Lighter Terminal B (Berths 2–4) is part of Intels Nigeria's Onne operation, concessioned 2006–2031. Intels built the "one-stop oil service centre" model at Onne, integrating berthing, yards, warehousing and free-zone logistics for the upstream industry, and FLT B is the lighter/inner-harbour component of that system.

Intels' corporate history (including its politically prominent ownership history and its past agency-fee disputes with the federal government) makes the company layer especially important here: control changes at Intels propagate across six registry facilities in four ports.

terminals.name: Federal Ocean Terminal A

point.note: This is the parent port's coordinate, not the facility's. The facility is known to be within the port complex, and nothing finer is established.

terminals.brief:
Federal Ocean Terminal A (Berths 1–6) is the deep-water core of Intels' Onne operation and functionally the most important oil-and-gas cargo berth system in Nigeria: rig moves, subsea hardware, casing, project cargo and offshore-supply logistics for the Niger Delta and Gulf of Guinea route through here. The Intels FOT concession runs 2006–2031.

Monitoring FOT A vessel calls gives a near-real-time read on upstream activity levels — drilling campaigns and field developments show up here as OSV and heavy-lift traffic before they show up in production data. This berth cluster is also the logical geographic anchor for the wider FOT jetty ecosystem (cement, fertiliser, LNG, repair).

terminals.name: Federal Ocean Terminal B (WACT)

point.note: This is the parent port's coordinate, not the facility's. The facility is known to be within the port complex, and nothing finer is established.

terminals.brief:
West Africa Container Terminal (Berths 7–8 at FOT) is the containerised face of Onne, concessioned 2007–2032 and operationally part of the APM Terminals network — a corporate linkage worth recording since it gives Maersk-affiliated operations both of eastern Nigeria's principal box berths. WACT competes for southeastern hinterland cargo that would otherwise route through Lagos, and free-zone adjacency gives it a role in oil-industry containerised supply.

Its growth is a useful indicator of trade decentralisation away from Lagos; berth-level specifications beyond operator/berth identity are not publicly verified in this registry.

terminals.name: Federal Ocean Terminal C (ICTSNL)

point.note: This is the parent port's coordinate, not the facility's. The facility is known to be within the port complex, and nothing finer is established.

terminals.brief:
Federal Ocean Terminal C (Berths 9–11) is operated by ICTS Nigeria (ICTSNL), the newest of the Onne container capacity tranches, associated in industry reporting with the ICTSI global terminal network — verify and record. Its concession record was not captured in the source material, an honest gap flagged in the registry.

Together with WACT it constitutes the eastern container gateway; watching allocation of services between the two reveals carrier strategy for eastern Nigeria. All marine specifications require sourcing.
terminals.notes: Concession record not captured in sources

terminals.name: New Terminal A
terminals.operator: Intels Nigeria Ltd (current operator to verify)

point.note: This is the parent port's coordinate, not the facility's. The facility is known to be within the port complex, and nothing finer is established.

terminals.brief:
Calabar New Terminal A was concessioned to Intels (June 2007–June 2032) as a container/general operation on Berths 1–2, though the registry flags that current operating control requires verification — Calabar's commercial activity has fluctuated severely with channel-draft constraints, and operator arrangements have evolved.

The terminal's fortunes are effectively a function of dredging: with adequate channel depth Calabar competes for southeastern cargo; without it, traffic defaults to Onne and Lagos. Channel status should be a linked live variable for this record.

terminals.name: New Terminal B

point.note: This is the parent port's coordinate, not the facility's. The facility is known to be within the port complex, and nothing finer is established.

terminals.brief:
Ecomarine Terminals operates Calabar New Terminal B (Berths 3–4) under the longest-running concession in the registry — commenced August 2007 and extended to 2037 per ICRC — handling container, general and liquid-bulk cargo. The extension makes Ecomarine the outlier in the 2031–2032 maturity cluster and signals a negotiated restructuring worth documenting in the concession layer.

Liquid-bulk capability ties the berth into regional petroleum-products distribution; as with all Calabar records, channel draft is the binding operational variable.

terminals.name: Old Terminal

point.note: This is the parent port's coordinate, not the facility's. The facility is known to be within the port complex, and nothing finer is established.

terminals.brief:
The Old Terminal at Calabar, operated by Shoreline Logistics (concession May 2007–May 2032), works the Milero and Jackson jetties with general and liquid-bulk cargo, carrying forward infrastructure from the port's historical Addax petroleum relationship. It is the legacy quay of the complex, older and shallower than the New Terminal berths.

Its liquid-bulk role and jetty-based configuration make it more akin to the marine-facility layer than a modern terminal; verify berth condition and current activity level before operational use.

terminals.name: Terminal A — Old Port Warri

point.note: This is the parent port's coordinate, not the facility's. The facility is known to be within the port complex, and nothing finer is established.

terminals.brief:
Terminal A at Old Port Warri is Intels' western-Delta multipurpose operation (Berths 1–3), an extension of the company's oil-service-centre model to the Warri river system. Old Port Warri handles general and oil-industry cargo for the western Delta at river drafts.

The Warri Intels berths complete the picture of Intels as a four-port national logistics network; concession documentation for the Delta berths was not captured in sources and is a registry gap.

terminals.name: Terminal B — Old Port Warri

point.note: This is the parent port's coordinate, not the facility's. The facility is known to be within the port complex, and nothing finer is established.

terminals.brief:
Terminal B at Old Port Warri is operated by Ocean & Cargo Terminal Services, a multipurpose river-berth operation in the canal/old-port area. Little is publicly documented beyond the NPA operator listing — an honest thin record.

offshore.name: Forcados Oil Terminal

point.note: Reliable facility location; the exact coordinate still needs confirmation.

offshore.brief:
Forcados is one of Nigeria's largest crude export systems, loading the medium-sweet Forcados grade through SPM infrastructure off the Forcados River mouth, with historically recorded shore storage of ~6.29m bbl (historical figure, requires current validation). Operated within the Shell/SPDC system and fed by the Trans-Forcados pipeline network, it has been the country's most incident-defined terminal: repeated force majeures from sabotage (including a 2016 subsea-line bombing costing an estimated $1bn in three months) and the 2022 discovery of a years-long illegal tap on feeder infrastructure.

Recent loading programmes place Forcados exports around 183,000 b/d (Nov 2025 schedule). For Seaphore, its operational state — loading, restricted, or under force majeure — is a headline national-revenue indicator, and its record should link pipeline-incident, AIS tanker-queue and force-majeure event feeds.

Chevron's deep-draft jetty infrastructure in the same locality (18 m) distinguishes Escravos from most Delta terminals. Model as the crude half of a dual oil/gas complex, cross-linked to NG-OFF-028 / NG-LNG-004.

The onshore terminal at Ibeno loads tankers through offshore SPMs and serves the Mobil-operated shallow-water production complex including Yoho and Usari.

Loadings on the Nov 2025 programme ran ~158,000 b/d. Its eastern location gives it a distinct risk profile from the Delta creeks — open-water piracy exposure and community/industrial action rather than creek theft — and its performance is a proxy for ExxonMobil's Nigerian shallow-water position.

Nov 2025 programmes scheduled Bonny Light around 180,000 b/d. Its records should link tightly to the Bonny fairway security picture shared with NLNG and to trunk-line incident feeds — the terminal is where Delta pipeline crime becomes visible in export data.

lngGas.name: Nigeria LNG Terminal

point.note: Facility-level coordinate, verified or near-verified.

lngGas.brief:
The Nigeria LNG complex at Finima, Bonny Island, is sub-Saharan Africa's largest gas-liquefaction facility and the single most valuable maritime-adjacent industrial asset in Nigeria. Operated by Nigeria LNG Ltd — a joint venture of NNPC, Shell, TotalEnergies and Eni — the plant has run since 1999 and now operates six trains totalling 22 mtpa of LNG plus around 5 mtpa of LPG and condensate, shipped from two dedicated LNG jetties by a fleet of dedicated carriers (6,000+ cargoes delivered to date). The Train 7 expansion (FID December 2019; ~80% construction by mid-2025) adds a seventh train and common liquefaction unit to lift capacity ~35% to 30 mtpa, with a new jetty and marine offloading facility in scope.

For Seaphore, NLNG is a distinct facility class with its own vessel population (LNG carriers on liner-like schedules), its own marine exclusion and security regime on the Bonny fairway, and a feedstock dependency on upstream Delta gas that ties its export performance to pipeline-security conditions well inland. Berth occupancy and carrier movements here are high-signal national economic indicators.

lngGas.brief:
One of two LNG-class jetties recorded at the Onne/FOT area serving gas-carrier and LNG-related traffic within the Bonny/Onne estuary system. Distinct from the NLNG export jetties at Finima, these facilities support the gas-logistics dimension of the Onne free-zone ecosystem; port-centroid coordinates only — facility-level geometry pending verification.

Treat as part of the Onne energy-jetty cluster for mapping and analytics: its traffic is specialised, intermittent and best interpreted alongside the adjacent LNG Jetty II and BRT condensate facilities rather than as a standalone terminal.

lngGas.brief:
The second LNG-class jetty in the Onne/FOT area, handling LNG and butane per the NPA facility listing. Together with LNG Jetty I it forms the gas-handling niche of the Onne jetty ecosystem, serving smaller gas carriers and butane/LPG distribution trades rather than the large export carriers that load at Bonny.

LPG throughput is a growing national trade as Nigeria pushes domestic cooking-gas penetration, making butane-capable berths increasingly relevant; verify current operational status and operator before relying on this record for scheduling analytics.

lngGas.brief:
Chevron's Escravos gas terminal is the gas-processing and export face of the Escravos complex, associated with the Escravos gas plant and gas-to-liquids operations. It is functionally distinct from the adjacent crude terminal: its flows are gas, LPG and GTL products, and its infrastructure has historically been a sabotage target with national power-supply consequences when the Escravos–Lagos pipeline system is disrupted.

Cross-listed with the offshore register (NG-OFF-028): model as one physical complex with two cargo systems. Deep-draft Chevron jetties (18 m) in the same locality give the complex unusual large-vessel capability for the western Delta.

lngGas.brief:
The Bonny export terminal jetty handles condensate and NLNG-associated liquids on Bonny Island, complementing the main LNG jetties. Condensate is a commercially significant sidestream of the NLNG system (stabilised and exported in parallel with LNG), and this jetty is the marine interface for that trade.

Approximate coordinates only; verify berth identity against NLNG's marine facilities (which include condensate storage and a materials-offloading facility) before treating this as an independent terminal in analytics.
